text: A man points a camera at his own life and waits for the footage to explain him. Comedy and drama, says the listing, and that is the first thing to notice: the diary is written, the confessions are composed, and seventy-four minutes of apparently raw record are a fiction pretending to be evidence. Jim McBride's joke is that the equipment keeps generating evasions — a camera used to postpone a decision, a tape recorder that catches everything except the point. Calling it an ancestor of reality television and the video diary, as the file does, makes it sound like a prophecy; it plays more like a diagnosis. A man performs sincerity for a machine he owns, then treats the performance as progress. That the National Film Registry now preserves the result is a fate the character inside it would have found entirely appropriate.

The film stock is three-quarters of an inch wide, and the camera that exposed it fed the strip sideways. Newark Athlete lasts one minute. William K.L. Dickson shot it in 1891 with an experimental horizontal-feed kinetograph and a viewer built to match, measurements chosen for a trial rather than a standard, and what he pointed the machine at was an athlete — the least complicated thing a body can do in front of a lens, motion repeated and legible without any need for a story. It sits on the National Film Registry as a document of hardware. Watching it is nearer to reading a specification than to seeing a film, though the minute is enough to notice how much of what came later was settled by the width of a ribbon and the direction it travelled.

A son comes home from the war and finds the marriage he grew up inside still running, badly. Three people, one Bronx apartment, the fighting just over: Ulu Grosbard holds to that arithmetic for a hundred and seven minutes, and the pressure comes from the impossibility of leaving a room without the argument following into the kitchen. The quarrels are household procedure here, grievances rehearsed across twenty years, politeness deployed as the sharper weapon. Timmy is the occasion rather than the subject; what his parents want from him is a witness, and each has a version of the past that requires his agreement. An Academy Award for Best Actress came out of it, which names the right thing for once: the interest lies in what a face does while somebody else is talking.

Thirteen minutes of moving water, and the night it happens in was manufactured with a red filter. Kenneth Anger took his camera to the fountains of the Villa d'Este at Tivoli and shot the Baroque waterworks so that the light comes back blue and the stone reads as something between marble and weather. A woman in elaborate dress moves through the terraces with evident purpose. Vivaldi's Winter plays. Nobody speaks, and the film treats that as sufficient. In place of narrative it matches rhythms — a cut, a jet rising, a descending violin phrase — until the figure among the statuary seems to be following the plumbing rather than any path of her own. Anger's own word for the thing was water games, and the pleasure on offer is a firework's rather than a story's: designed, timed, over.

Fifteen days before a national election, a candidate's daughter stops coming home. The campaign does not stop. Lee Kyoung-mi builds her thriller on that collision: a house in which a missing girl and a polling schedule compete for the same hours, and a wife who must decide how much of her husband's business she is prepared to understand. The search she conducts herself leads into her daughter's ordinary life, which turns out to be a country she never visited. Electoral machinery supplies the tempo, all deadlines and managed appearances; the marriage supplies the damage. What holds the hundred and two minutes together is tone — brackish, unembarrassed by melodrama, hostile to the notion that a family scandal can be handled properly. KOFA counts it among a hundred Korean films.

Lewis Tater writes Wild West novels for the dime trade, then goes west to live inside his own material. Nothing out there matches the prose. Howard Zieff's comedy runs on that gap: a man who learned the frontier from paperbacks, arriving in a place where the first people to take an interest in him are two crooks trying to rob him, and leaving with their box of money by accident. The joke could be cruel and largely isn't. Tater's ambition — to become the figure he has been describing for money — is treated as a reasonable thing to want, and the film keeps a straight face while the territory declines to cooperate. A hundred and two minutes, half western and half sales pitch. The National Board of Review put it among the ten best of 1975.

At eighty, Alice Hargreaves crosses to New York to be thanked for having once been somebody's inspiration. The reception at Columbia University is in Lewis Carroll's honour; she is the surviving evidence. Gavin Millar uses the licence of fantasy sparingly and pointedly — the Wonderland creatures arrive as pressure rather than decoration, showing up when the old woman's account of that friendship stops being charming to her. Two versions coexist: the story she has told all her life, and the one she is beginning to believe. The film is patient with the distance between them, and precise about the position of a child given an attention she had no words for. Ninety-four minutes, English childhood and American ceremony, neither explaining the other. The National Board of Review listed it among 1985's ten best.

Stones move, mud pots spit, and flowers open on ground that looked at first like nothing but grit. Sixty-nine minutes are built on that reversal. The Living Desert takes long stretches of patient field photography and cuts them for suspense, so that a lizard and a snake acquire the timing of an ambush and a bubbling pot of mud becomes a gag with a punchline; the narration is confident, the score comments freely, and the animals are assigned intentions they may or may not hold. That is the method and also the argument — that a desert will support the attention normally reserved for drama. It took the Academy's documentary award for 1953, nature photography arranged as entertainment rather than instruction, and whether the arrangement is fair to its subjects is the live question in it.

A missed train, a station cafe, and a stranger at the table eating the salad she just paid for. Twelve minutes, one concourse, a great many people with somewhere else to be. Adam Davidson's short is an exercise in seating: who sits, who stands, who is entitled to object out loud, and how quickly a shared table becomes a jurisdiction. Very little is said. The negotiations happen in a fork set down, a glance measured, the etiquette of a public room doing work that dialogue would flatten, and the camera stays inside the woman's assumptions rather than correcting them, which is where both the comedy and the discomfort come from. It won the Academy Award for live action short. Its whole method is patience — waiting for a viewer to reach a thought a moment before the film confirms it.

Morning on the harbour, and a ferry unloads its crowd at the foot of the island. Eleven minutes later the light is going off the water again. Charles Sheeler's 1921 film has no story and nobody to follow, only positions: a view straight down onto Wall Street, ranks of towers venting steam, an ironworker steady on a high beam, a locomotive readied in its yard, a liner nudged into place by tugs. The framing carries the argument — the city seen past a balustrade, the city as columns and diagonals, foot traffic reduced to a dark current between blocks. Lines of Walt Whitman appear between shots with his name withheld, so the words behave like captions instead of authority. A working day, described by someone chiefly interested in geometry, and New York obliges by looking built rather than grown.

Two-color Technicolor could deliver reds and blue-greens and almost nothing else, and the sets of King of Jazz were designed to live inside that limit. There is no plot. Paul Whiteman and his orchestra stand at the centre of a hundred-minute revue of numbers, sketches and tableaux, staged with the scale of a theatre evening and the fixity of a camera still working out what sound would let it do. The Academy gave the film its award for production design, which is the honest verdict: what lasts is the architecture the performers are placed in — staircases, outsized props, painted depth, all of it built for a palette rather than a story. Hollywood in 1930, testing whether an entire stage bill could be crated up and shipped to every town with a screen. The seams of the test show in every transition.

Kansas in the 1920s, a small town, and the months in which a Black teenager is no longer permitted to be a child. Gordon Parks made the film in 1969, and its method is accumulation rather than crisis: a household's loyalties and its grudges, ambitions stated once and quietly revised, the ordinary transactions of a place where the rules that matter are not the written ones. Nothing is enlarged for effect. The adults are neither saints nor lessons, and the boy's education comes mostly from watching which offences get punished and which get absorbed. Less than a year passes; it is enough to finish the job. The National Film Registry holds it. What sounds like calm in the film is nothing of the kind — it is a town where raising a voice costs something everyone present can price.

Kurt Anderson runs a New York department store the way a garrison is run under siege, and in 1933 the siege is the economy. Seventy-five minutes, spent mostly on the sales floor and in the office above it: a manager who dismisses a man after twenty years without breaking stride, who treats the women he hires as another line in the ledger, and whom the film watches closely without hurrying to correct him. Madeline needs work badly enough to spend a night obtaining it, then falls for a young man rising inside the same building, and her fear is not exposure in the abstract but the exact arithmetic of what he would make of it. Hiring, humiliation and romance all happen in the same corridors here. The speed is part of the meaning: nobody in the building has time to be decent.

The assignment was to make an ally legible: the Soviet Union, at war with Germany, explained to American audiences in eighty-three minutes. Fifth in Frank Capra's Why We Fight series, the film works by compilation and map — footage shot by other people, a front line redrawn until it becomes a diagram anybody can follow, geography first and then invasion and then the sheer size of what the Eastern Front was consuming. The mode is briefing, not inquiry. It is instructive to follow how the persuasion is assembled, the cut that converts a statistic into a threat, the music that tells a listener what to feel about a river. The Academy gave it the documentary award for 1943. Capra's name sits strangely on it, and the strangeness is the point: familiar instincts, aimed at propaganda's flat requirements.
